title: Everything for Life and Godliness, and the Sure Word
summary: Peter greets those who share a faith as precious as the apostles' and reminds them that God's power has given them everything needed for life and godliness, so that they may share in the divine nature. They must therefore add to their faith a growing chain of virtues ending in love, confirming their calling and election. Knowing his death is near, Peter writes to remind them of these things, grounding his message in what he saw at the transfiguration and in the prophetic word, which came from God as men were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
story: Second Peter presents itself as the apostle's farewell, written as his death approached, probably to the same churches addressed in 1 Peter (3:1). Where 1 Peter strengthened believers facing hostility from outside, 2 Peter strengthens them against a danger from inside: teachers who deny Christ's return and turn freedom into license, whom chapter 2 will expose. Before the warning comes the foundation. Chapter 1 sets out what God has given, what believers must pursue, and why the apostolic message can be trusted, reaching back to the transfiguration, when Peter, James, and John saw Jesus' glory, and to the prophets of Israel.
historical:
The letter's authorship and date are among the most debated questions in the New Testament (see the introduction). If Peter wrote it, verse 14 reflects his awareness that his death was near, in keeping with Jesus' prediction in John 21:18-19, and it dates to the mid-60s AD, shortly before his execution in Rome under Nero. Many scholars instead read the chapter as a testament written in Peter's name after his death, using the familiar form of a farewell speech to preserve his teaching for a later generation, perhaps late in the first century or early in the second.

The transfiguration Peter recalls in verses 16-18 is recorded in Matthew 17:1-8, Mark 9:2-8, and Luke 9:28-36, where Jesus is transformed before Peter, James, and John on a high mountain and the Father's voice declares him his beloved Son. The Gospels do not name the mountain; later tradition identified it with Mount Tabor in Galilee, and some modern scholars suggest Mount Hermon. Peter calls it “the holy mountain” because of what happened there.
cultural:
Several of the chapter's words come from the vocabulary of Greek moral philosophy and religion. Virtue (aretē), self-control, godliness, and knowledge were ideals discussed by philosophers across the Greek world, and lists of virtues were a familiar form of moral teaching. Peter uses this language to address readers in their own terms, but he fills it with new content: the list begins with faith and ends with love, and the power to pursue it comes from God. The idea of sharing the divine nature also had echoes in Greek religious thought, though Peter's meaning is shaped by the promises of God and escape from corruption, not by the absorption of the self into the divine.

The cleverly devised fables (muthoi) of verse 16 recall the myths of the Greek gods, stories that educated people of the time often treated as poetic inventions. The false teachers apparently dismissed the apostles' message about Christ's coming in power as a myth of that kind. Peter replies by appealing to eyewitness testimony, the strongest kind of evidence in ancient law and history writing. His description of his body as a tent recalls the temporary dwellings of Israel in the wilderness and perhaps the tents he wanted to build on the mountain of transfiguration (Mark 9:5).
literary: The chapter follows the pattern of a farewell testament: a greeting, a summary of the essential message, the speaker's awareness of his coming death, the purpose of leaving a reminder, and warnings about the future (which follow in chapter 2). Verses 5-7 form a chain in which each virtue is added to the one before, a rhetorical form sometimes called a climax or sorites, also used by Paul in Romans 5:3-5. It rises from faith to love. The words remind and memory recur in verses 12-15, stressing that the readers already know the truth. The chapter closes with two witnesses to the truth of Christ's coming: the apostolic eyewitnesses (verses 16-18) and the prophetic Scriptures (verses 19-21), with the image of a lamp shining in a dark place until the day dawns.

outline.t: God's power and promises: sharing the divine nature
Adding virtue to faith, and confirming one's calling

doctrines.note: God's divine power has given “everything we need for life and godliness”, and through his promises believers “become partakers of the divine nature”. Salvation is both God's gift and an invitation to growth, and those who grow in virtue “make your calling and election sure”, not by earning it but by confirming it in life.

“No such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.” Scripture is both human speech and God's word, spoken by real people through the Spirit's guidance.
The virtues of verses 5-7 describe a growing likeness to God that begins with faith and culminates in love. Their absence leaves a person nearsighted and forgetful of the cleansing they received.
Jesus is called “our God and Savior Jesus Christ” (verse 1) and the Father's beloved Son (verse 17). The transfiguration shows his majesty and points forward to his coming in power.

words.note: Epignōsis, knowledge or full knowledge, especially personal acquaintance. It appears in verses 2, 3, and 8. The knowledge of God and of Jesus is the channel through which grace, peace, and everything needed for godliness come. The false teachers may have claimed special knowledge; Peter insists true knowledge is of a person and bears fruit.

Phusis, nature. The phrase partakers of the divine nature is one of the boldest in the New Testament. Eastern Orthodox theology has drawn on it for the doctrine of theosis (deification), meaning union with God by grace without ceasing to be creatures. Western traditions usually read it as sharing God's moral character and immortality through union with Christ. All agree it does not mean becoming God in essence.

Epoptēs, eyewitness, one who has seen something personally. The word was also used in Greek religion for a higher grade of initiate in the mystery cults, but here it has its plain sense: Peter and the other apostles saw Christ's majesty with their own eyes.

Pherō, to bear or carry. It appears four times in this chapter: the voice was borne from the Majestic Glory (verse 17), and prophecy was not brought by human will, but men spoke as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (verse 21). The image, used elsewhere of a ship driven by the wind (Acts 27:15, 17), pictures the prophets moved by the Spirit while still speaking as themselves.

christ: The chapter begins with one of the clearest statements of Christ's deity in the New Testament, “our God and Savior Jesus Christ”, where the Greek grammar most naturally applies both titles to Jesus. It centers on the transfiguration, where Peter saw Jesus' majesty and heard the Father declare, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”, echoing Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1. That glimpse of glory is, for Peter, a preview and guarantee of Christ's coming in power. Christ is also the one who revealed Peter's death to him (verse 14), the object of the knowledge that makes believers fruitful, and the King of the eternal kingdom into which they will be richly welcomed. The morning star rising in believers' hearts (verse 19) probably refers to Christ himself, whose coming brings the full day (compare Numbers 24:17; Revelation 22:16).

hard.q: What does it mean that “no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation”?
hard.a: The phrase can be read in two main ways. On the first, it concerns the origin of prophecy: the prophets did not produce their messages from their own interpretation of events or visions, since, as verse 21 explains, their words came from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. This reading fits the flow of verses 20-21 and is favored by many interpreters. On the second, it concerns how readers interpret prophecy: no individual may interpret Scripture in isolation or by private whim, but should read it with the guidance of the Spirit and within the community of faith. Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions have often drawn on this reading in support of the church's teaching authority, while Protestant traditions emphasize that Scripture is its own best interpreter, though all agree Scripture should not be twisted to suit individual preference (as 3:16 warns). The two readings are not entirely opposed: if prophecy comes from God, it must be read as God's word and not bent to human purposes.

questions: Peter says God has given everything needed for life and godliness, yet calls believers to make every effort. How do God's gift and human effort fit together in your life?
Which virtue in the chain of verses 5-7 is most lacking in you right now, and what would it mean to add it?
Peter grounds his hope in eyewitness testimony and prophetic Scripture. What gives you confidence that the message about Jesus is not a clever myth?
